gallery.title: File:Shezade mosque 9195.jpg
gallery.description: To the east of the mosque and accessible from the north garden as well as along the south with a small path there is a set of mausolea that, although often closed (but luckily increasingly often opened, they used to be closed always), are well worth a visit. Inside some of them are excellent Iznik tiles from the best periods. The Strolling through Istanbul guidebook stresses that they span a wider range of time then the mausolea at the Hagia Sophia.

gallery.title: File:Shezade mosque 4866.jpg
gallery.description: To the left the wall surrounding a garden that often can be entered through a gate, inside the garden are the great mausolea and graves. There is an exit to the north of the garden where the picture was taken through another small gate, leading past remains of the viaduct of Valens and on.

gallery.title: File:Shezade mosque 9510.jpg
gallery.description: In the article for this mosque it is stated that the use of four semi-domes around the central one " .... was not entirely successful, as it isolated the four huge piers needed to support the central dome, and was never again repeated by Sinan. " Strolling through Istanbul (guidebook) agrees, but gives as another reason "the identical symmetry along both axes has a repetitive effect which tends towards dulness."

gallery.title: File:Shezade mosque 9205.jpg
gallery.description: Though complaints can be uttered regarding the huge size of the columns, they are well-adorned and pieces of art in themselves.

gallery.title: File:Istanbul Şehzade complex Tomb of Rüstem Paşa in 2023 3831.jpg
gallery.source: Istanbul Şehzade complex Tomb of Rüstem Paşa in 2023 3831
gallery.description: This is the mausoleum of grand vizier Rüstem Paşa, who died in 1561. Architect was Sinan. The Strolling through Istanbul book is critical on both its design and its tiles. The building is seen as “too high for its diameter and too small to support the overwhelming quantity of tiles”. These tiles are described as being from about ten years before the Iznik tile production and its Armenian bole reached perfection. I always found it closed, so only took a picture through a window.

gallery.source: Istanbul Şehzade complex Tomb of Şehzade Mehmed interior Cuerda seca tiles in 2015 1380
gallery.description: Much of the decoration is with tiles in a technique that was introduced to Iznik in about 1514 when Selim I brought Persian craftsmen after conquering Tabriz. The latest examples are from 1555 in the Kara Ahmet Paşa mosque. This türbe contains the most extensive and beautiful collection in this style.

gallery.description: Imaret is generally translated as soup kitchen or public kitchen. This is, across a street from the mosque’s garden wall, the imaret of the Şehzade complex, now used by an organisation called Siyasal Vakfı (Political Foundation). Its garden is well-kept, and some pictures show one of the dining rooms and some of the remains of its cooking area.

gallery.title: File:Şehzade cami (1).jpg
gallery.description:
Şehzade Mosque, a 16th-century Ottoman imperial mosque located in the district of Fatih, on the third hill of Istanbul, Turkey.
It was commissioned by Suleiman the Magnificent as a memorial to his favorite son Şehzade Mehmed who died in 1543. It is sometimes referred to as the "Prince's Mosque" in English.

Suleiman is said to have personally mourned the death of Mehmed for forty days at his temporary tomb in Istanbul, the site upon which the imperial architect Mimar Sinan would construct a lavish mausoleum to Mehmed as one part of a larger mosque complex dedicated to the princely heir. The complex was Sinan's first important imperial commission and ultimately one of his most ambitious architectural works, even though it was designed early in his long career.
